Because of this, Cicero clashed with him—a conflict that did not come out into the open, but caused their friendly treatment of one another to become noticeably cooler.

XXXV. After this, Clodius was killed by Milo; and being prosecuted for murder, he engaged Cicero as his advocate. The Senate, fearing that a disturbance might arise in the city during the trial of Milo—who was a man of high repute and spirit—entrusted the oversight of this and the other trials to Pompey, to ensure the security of the city and the courts. Pompey, while it was still night, posted his soldiers on the heights to surround the forum. Milo, fearing that Cicero might be unsettled by the unusual sight and conduct his case less effectively, persuaded him to be carried to the forum in a litter and to wait there quietly until the jurors gathered and the courtroom was full. 

Now Cicero, as it seems, was not only cowardly when under arms, but also felt fear when he began to speak; in many trials, he could hardly stop shaking and trembling even when his eloquence had reached its peak and settled into its flow. Once, when defending Licinius Murena against a case brought by Cato, he was so ambitious to surpass Hortensius, who had delivered a successful plea, that he did not rest at all during the night. Consequently, he was so harmed by his extreme anxiety and lack of sleep that he appeared inferior to his usual self.

*ἐφεξῆς* [In order]. Furthermore, he introduces a false doctrine; for in the Diatonic genus, three tones are placed in succession, from the *meson diatonos* to the *paramesos*: however, not in one tetrachord. Hence I thought it should be read, *καθ᾿ ἕν τεράχορδον* [in one tetrachord], as indicated in the translation.

V. 19. *πείσαται*] So all three codices read; but beyond doubt, poorly. I restore the reading, *παρίσταται*. It is brought into dissonance.

V. 21. The Oxford [codices], *μὲν εἰσίν*.

Ibid. *πυκνὰ μὲν τὰ ἐλάχιστα* [Dense are the smallest (intervals)],] Capella translates these less clearly at v. 25: *Those are dense which are gathered by dieses; rarer, those by tones.*

V. 24. *τᾶ δ᾿ ἑνόνος*] Thus corruptly in all three codices; and additionally in the Codices of the Royal Library at Paris. Yet the sense itself cries out that it must be read *δι-τόνου* [of the ditone], as indicated in the translation.

...first happened to the Athenians. Inaros, son of Psammetichus, a Libyan king of the Libyans bordering on Egypt, operating from Marea, the city above Pharos, caused most of Egypt to revolt from King Artaxerxes. Becoming ruler himself, he brought in the Athenians. They, being already on an expedition to Cyprus with two hundred ships of their own and their allies, abandoned Cyprus and sailed up from the sea into the Nile. Controlling the river and two parts of Memphis, they fought against the third part, which is called the White Wall; inside were the Persians and Medes who had taken refuge, along with those Egyptians who had not joined the revolt. The Athenians landed at Halieis, where a battle took place against the Corinthians and Epidaurians, and the Corinthians were victorious. Later, the Athenians fought a sea battle off Cecryphaleia against Peloponnesian ships, and the Athenians were victorious. When war broke out between the Athenians and the Aeginetans, a great sea battle occurred off Aegina between the Athenians and the Aeginetans; allies were present on both sides, and the Athenians were victorious. Having captured seventy of their ships, they landed on the island and besieged it, under the command of Leocrates, son of Stroebus. Then the Peloponnesians, wishing to assist the Aeginetans, transported three hundred hoplites of the Corinthians and Epidaurians to Aegina as reinforcements. They occupied the heights of Geraneia and descended into the Megarid, thinking the Athenians would be unable to assist the Megarians, as a large force was away in Aegina and Egypt, or that if they did assist, they would have to withdraw from Aegina. The Athenians did not move their force from Aegina, but from those remaining in the city, the oldest and the youngest, they arrived at Megara under the command of Myronides. A battle, which was evenly matched, occurred against the Corinthians, and they separated; each side thought they had not fared the worse in the encounter. The Athenians, however, having gained the upper hand, set up a trophy after the Corinthians departed. The Corinthians, being reproached by the elders in their city, prepared themselves for about twelve days, returned, and set up a trophy of their own, claiming victory. The Athenians, sallying forth from Megara, killed those who were setting up the trophy and, engaging the others, were victorious. Those who were defeated retreated. A not insignificant portion of them, pressured and having lost their way, fell into the private property of an individual, which happened to be surrounded by a large trench, and there was no exit. The Athenians, realizing this, blocked them in front with their hoplites, surrounded them with light-armed troops, and stoned to death all who had entered. This was a great disaster for the Corinthians, and the bulk of their army returned home. At this time, the Athenians began to build their Long Walls to the sea, one to Phalerum and the other to Piraeus. When the Phocians campaigned against the Dorians—the mother-city of the Lacedaemonians—Boius, Cytinium, and Erineus, and captured one of these small cities, the Lacedaemonians, under the leadership of Nicomedes, son of Cleombrotus, on behalf of Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, who was still a minor, assisted the Dorians with fifteen hundred hoplites of their own and ten thousand of their allies. After forcing the Phocians to return the city under an agreement, they retreated. By sea, the Athenians had sailed around with ships and intended to prevent them if they wished to cross through the Crisaean Gulf; by way of Geraneia, it did not seem safe to them, as the Athenians held Megara and Pegae. Geraneia is a difficult pass and was always guarded by the Athenians, and they knew they would try to block them there. It seemed best to them to remain in Boeotia to consider how they might cross most safely. Some of the Athenians were also inciting them secretly, hoping to put an end to the democracy and the Long Walls being built. The Athenians marched out against them with their entire force, supported by one thousand Argives and their other allies, each as they could, amounting in total to fourteen thousand. Thinking they were at a loss as to how to pass, they marched against them. Also, some came under suspicion of planning to dissolve the democracy. Thessalian cavalry also arrived for the Athenians according to the alliance, who changed sides in the heat of the battle to the Lacedaemonians. A battle took place at Tanagra in Boeotia, and the Lacedaemonians and their allies were victorious; there was great slaughter on both sides. The Lacedaemonians went into the Megarid, cut down the trees, and departed home again through Geraneia and the Isthmus. The Athenians, on the sixty-second day after the battle, marched into Boeotia...

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical investigation into the nature of matter and form, specifically addressing the arguments found in Plotinus's second Ennead, fourth tractate. It bridges the discussion from the "rational principles" of the previous page to the specific "formlessness" of matter.</meta>

# Ennead II. 4

### On Matter

It takes something of another along with itself within its own **form**. But there is a difficulty <note>original: *aporia* — a philosophical state of being at a loss or facing an unsolvable contradiction.</note>; he says again that it was not found in any direct application. And since this is not a proof, we shall take the reception of the **form**, as though it were not in itself, to be what produces the form. He will show that the form is **infinite** <note>original: *apeiron* — meaning unbounded or lacking limit; a central concept in Neoplatonic views on matter.</note>. Whatever happens to be of the same nature occurs when the form is absent. For it participates in form because of itself, since it is infinite; and that which is stable belongs to form, though not as a promise, but as it exists within the forms; for that which is upon it...

Indeed, he says that this is the case: that not all living things participate, in which there is no **being** <note>original: *einai* — the state of true existence as opposed to mere becoming.</note>, but rather there is that which made things together with them. This does not create a type <note>original: *typon* — an imprint or stamp, like a seal in wax.</note>; and they are not so called; they are infinite when neither one nor the other exists. But it is within; the reason is that it participates in **formlessness** <note>original: *amorphia*</note>. Some things are everything. Some things are impossible. Others, again, are **otherness** <note>original: *heterotes* — the principle of being "different" which Plotinus uses to explain how matter recedes from the One.</note>, not even the things that are impossible. Of these, some are accidental; again, they are the same. Or of what kind? Because it is not form itself. But because it is everything, it is itself. Or it is all things. Others, again, are what follows.

In that which is **matter** <note>original: *hyle*</note>, there is also the fact of being in these "angles" <note>likely a geometric metaphor for the specific positions or constraints of physical existence.</note>; for instance, not by the "not" but by the "different," or by the fact that not even the differing things, or the same things, exist. Or that, again, it is all or what follows. For that which is in these is not from itself, nor in all, nor in the whole, nor in a "where" that is not even a whole, but rather it is the things within. For the **rational principle** <note>term: *logos* — the formative, organizing force that flows from the Divine Intellect into matter.</note> is in the form. And there is no "still more," such as the things within being. But it is necessary for all things, even those without form within the form, to be the offspring of others or as much as is needed. But in the **infinite**, it belongs to the form.

There is, again, a reason regarding **matter** and being. That when what is in it is not there at all, they would neither possess essence nor would they **shine** <note>Plotinus frequently uses the metaphor of light: matter is a dark mirror that only "exists" when the light of the Forms reflects off it.</note>. But upon which it neither is nor exists, whenever it comes from motion or exists according to itself, or is not even as is likely. Individual things do not exist by being the same, as they are at a loss. Either the being of the **accidents** <note>original: *symbebekoton* — non-essential qualities that happen to a substance.</note> within it, or not even itself. But again, it is always becoming infinite. The remaining things of each. We might hold these ourselves. Those things which follow it suffered, and are created. Some will exceed; to have the same things; see how he always says: that...

The reason of **essence** <note>original: *ousia* — the true substance or "being-ness" of a thing.</note>. For if it is because it is into the most things, then the quality of good order is entirely something similar. Still, there is the matter of being left behind. It makes everything. It was said that it is either by the **reason** alone. He might say. Or since that which possesses that, how did it come through that one? Neither will those things be. Nor is it for all of them. Nor for those still upon them, because, and entirely. (As if both were everything; again it produces motion. Or to be entirely there as well. How, or where, or for all. Or where then will it be; because. Or how, or entirely. For what kind of things are those in the form? And will there be certain things of it, just as there is **matter**?

<summary>Plotinus explores the difficult relationship between Form and Matter, arguing that Matter is a formless "infinite" that only gains reality or "shines" when it participates in the Rational Principles (Logoi) of the intelligible realm.</summary>

I laugh at the human being. For them, things come to be, but they are empty of upright deeds, and they are numbed by all sorts of suggestions. Without any benefit, they grasp at endless toils, unraveling the limits of the earth and the boundless recesses of immoderate desire. They melt down silver and gold, and they do not cease from this acquisition, but are always disturbed, worrying how the greater part might become less for them. And they are not ashamed, when it is said, that they dig into the chasms of the earth with shackled hands. Some of them have perished upon the very surface of the earth, while others, over a long time, dwell in this necessity as if in their own homeland of punishment, searching for silver and gold, seeking out traces and nuggets, gathering sand from one place and another, cutting the veins of the earth, making themselves miserable for the sake of abundance from the earth. Yet they marvel at and trample upon the small, singular earth. How much they love the laborious and the hidden, while they insult their daily life. They purchase dogs, others horses, while others fence off much land and mark it as their own. Wanting to differ from many, they are unable to do so even from themselves. They rush to marry those whom they soon cast out. They love, then hate. They act with desire, then depart completely. What is this empty, irrational zeal, differing nothing from madness? Having made himself ruler, he called in the Athenians. They happened to be campaigning against Cyprus with two hundred ships of their own and of their allies. Leaving Cyprus, they came and sailed up from the sea into the Nile. Gaining control of the river and two parts of Memphis, they pressed on against the third part, which is called the White Fortress <note>the fortified citadel of Memphis</note>. Those of the Persians and Medes who had fled there were inside, along with those Egyptians who had not joined the revolt.

The Athenians, landing from their ships at Halieis, fought a battle against the Corinthians and Epidaurians, and the Corinthians won. Later the Athenians fought a naval battle off Cecryphaleia against the ships of the Peloponnesians, and the Athenians won.

When war was declared against the Aeginetans by the Athenians, a great naval battle took place off Aegina between the Athenians and the Aeginetans. The allies of each side were present, and the Athenians won. Taking seventy of their ships, they landed on the island and laid siege to it under the command of Leocrates son of Stroebus. Then the Peloponnesians, wishing to bring aid to the Aeginetans, sent across to Aegina three hundred hoplites who were previously mercenaries of the Corinthians and Epidaurians. The Corinthians with their allies seized the heights of Mount Geraneia and descended into the Megarid, believing it would be impossible for the Athenians to assist the Megarians, since a large force was absent at Aegina and in Egypt; or, if they did assist, they would have to withdraw from Aegina.

The Athenians did not move the army at Aegina. Instead, from those remaining in the city, both the oldest and the youngest, they came to Megara under the command of Myronides. After an indecisive battle was fought against the Corinthians, the two sides separated from one another, and each side considered that they had come off no worse in the engagement. The Athenians, who nevertheless had the upper hand, set up a trophy after the Corinthians departed. The Corinthians, reproached by the elders in their city and having spent about twelve days preparing, returned and set up a rival trophy themselves, claiming victory. The Athenians came out in force from Megara, killed those who were setting up the trophy, engaged the rest, and defeated them.

The defeated Corinthians began to retreat. A considerable portion of them, forced back and missing the road, fell into an enclosure belonging to a private citizen, which happened to be surrounded by a deep ditch with no way out. The Athenians, seeing this, blocked the entrance in front with their hoplites, and surrounding them on all sides with light-armed troops, stoned to death all who had entered. This was a great disaster for the Corinthians. The main body of their army retreated back home.

At this time the Athenians also began to build the Long Walls down to the sea, both the wall to Phalerum and the wall to Piraeus.

When the Phocians campaigned against Doris, the ancestral homeland of the Lacedaemonians—consisting of Boeum, Cytinium, and Erineum—and captured one of these small towns, the Lacedaemonians went to the aid of the Dorians. They brought fifteen hundred hoplites of their own and ten thousand of their allies. Having compelled the Phocians by treaty to surrender the town, they prepared to return. If they wished to cross by sea across the Crisaean Gulf, the Athenians were prepared to prevent them by sailing around with their fleet. Nor did marching through Mount Geraneia appear safe to them, since the Athenians held Megara and Pegae. Mount Geraneia is difficult to traverse and was continually guarded by the Athenians; and at that time they perceived that the Athenians intended to block them along that route.

<meta>This page continues the translation of Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book X, specifically from the section where the author distinguishes between the active, social life of a citizen and the superior, contemplative life of the philosopher. The previous page established that while practical virtue is noble, the "intellect" represents the highest part of the human being.</meta>

And just people wish to act justly, toward whomever they might act; and through both [the intention and the act] friendship exists. But which of these constitutes the essence of moral success? For indeed, the temperate person seeks **orderly conduct** <note>original: "eutaxian" — referring to a well-ordered or disciplined life</note>. For how would this person, or any other, be manifest to others without action? 

It is debated whether **moral choice** <term>proairesis</term> <note>the internal, deliberate intention or decision-making process behind a deed</note> or the actual deeds are more essential to virtue, since virtue seems to exist in both. It is clear, then, that perfection would reside in both. Yet actions require external things; and the greater and nobler the actions, the more external resources they require. In this way, they are beautiful; but the person seeking the path of the virtues does not even need "poets" <note>original: "poiētōn" — here likely used in the sense of "makers" or external producers to validate their virtue</note>. Simply put, the disposition of the soul according to its own impulse requires **external grace** <note>original: "charitos" — meaning favor, external support, or the equipment needed to manifest a virtue</note>. 

Indeed, choosing to live for the sake of reputation and honor is not the same as choosing to act rightly. A person will therefore need such external goods in order to live as a human being <note>Aristotle is arguing that because we are human, we cannot escape the need for food, money, and social standing, even if these aren't the highest goals</note>. But that **happiness** <term>eudaimonia</term> <note>the state of flourishing or living well; the ultimate human "good"</note> is **contemplative** <term>theoretike</term> <note>the activity of the mind observing truth, independent of physical action</note> — from where might this be clear? 

Let us consider the gods: we assume the gods to be, above all others, **blessed** <term>makarios</term> <note>a state of supreme, divine happiness</note> and happy. But what kind of actions should we attribute to them? Should we say they perform just actions? Or will they appear ridiculous if we imagine them making contracts and returning deposits, and doing all such things? But what about courageous actions? Do they endure terrifying things and face risks because it is noble to do so? Or what about liberal actions? To whom will they give? It is absurd to think of them having money or anything of the sort. And if they have their own interests, what would they be? Or would a god be temperate? Is not praise for such self-restraint trivial, since gods have no base desires to overcome? 

If we go through every case, all matters concerning physical actions appear petty and unworthy of the gods. Yet everyone says that the gods must be alive; and if they are alive, they must be active. For surely they are not sleeping like **Endymion** <note>In Greek mythology, the youth Endymion was granted eternal sleep by Zeus so that he would never age or die. Aristotle uses him as the ultimate example of a life that is "alive" but totally inactive.</note>. 

For a living being who is deprived of physical action, and even more so of "making" anything, what is left except **contemplation**? Thus, the activity of God, which excels in blessedness, must be contemplative. Consequently, among human activities, the one that is most closely related to this divine activity is the most happy. A sign of this is that other animals do not share in happiness, being entirely deprived of this kind of activity. For to the gods, the whole of life is blessed...

<summary>This page argues that true happiness is found in contemplation rather than physical action. By showing that human social virtues (like justice or courage) would be "ridiculous" if attributed to the gods, the author concludes that the highest, most divine form of life is the activity of the mind.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, ethics, happiness, eudaimonia, contemplation, theoretike, divine nature, moral choice, Endymion, virtue</keywords>

To those who examine all these matters, everything concerning actions appears small and unworthy of gods.

For surely they do not sleep like Endymion <note>Endymion was a figure in Greek mythology granted eternal sleep by Zeus so that he would never age</note>.
